newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ Post annual net profit falls to NZ$47.7 mln.
newsitem.headline: NZ Post annual net profit falls to NZ$47.7 mln.

text.p: State-owned postal service New Zealand Post on Wednesday reported a net after tax profit of NZ$47.7 million in the year to March 31, down 36.6 percent on last year's $75.2 million profit.
NZ Post said it paid a dividend to government, excluding special dividends, of $28.6 million in the 1997 year, down 36.6 percent from the previous year.
The total dividend for the year was $113.6 million, which included a special dividend of $85 million.
Last year's total dividend was $85.3 million, which included a $40.2 million special dividend paid following the sale of the Auckland Chief Post Office.
NZ Post said that a reduction in the standard letter price from 45 cents to 40 cents cost $35 million in revenue and a free post day cost $1.2 million in foregone revenue and additional expenses.
It also attributed the profit drop to a slower economy and said the high kiwi dollar affected international operations.
The profit was on turnover of $678 million, up 3.1 percent on last year. Expenditure of $613 million was up 11.3 percent and tax of $24.9 million, was down 17.8 percent.

The company argued the result was solid and that it would continue to be a viable business when the government carried through legislation which will remove New Zealand Post's present monopoly on standard letter delivery, expected to take effect some time in 1998.
Chief executive Elmar Toime said the company's performance would be affected by deregulation, but NZ Post supported the decision.
"We are confident about performing in a deregulated market. Our outlook is positive in all our business areas," he said.
He said the company had increased capital investment this year to $46.3 million from $33.8 million last year.
The benefits of this investment would be apparent now that deregulation of the last protected area in the postal market -- the standard letter -- was imminent.
Toime said the company was on a new plateau of profitability reflecting the lower prices NZ Post has been charging.
He said revenue had slowed in the last part of the 1996/97 year, and that would probably continue into the current fiscal year. However, the company still expected volume growth.
"Our growth expectations are lower but we expect to meet our business plan," Toime said.
NZ Post said it expected a 1997/98 year result "broadly in line with this year".
The company said it currently had no plans to increase the standard letter price and it would not reintroduce the rural delivery fee.
